analysis.title: The Pulse of the Market: Still on the Sidelines With Tech, More Midterm Thoughts, Getting More Constructive on Small Caps
key_insights: RBC stays at market weight on S&P 500 Technology after the Oct 14 downgrade from overweight, and reiterates overweight on Health Care. Since Oct 14, Health Care has been the top sector in the index and Tech the second worst, ahead of only Communication Services.

Tech valuations have improved and are slightly attractive on RBC's model, but the case is not deep. Semis valuations improved too, but EPS estimate revisions for Semiconductors & Semi Equipment are still decelerating. Tech fund flows look better on a four-week average only because of one sharp inflow several weeks ago that has since faded.

RBC turns constructive on Small Caps and prefers them to Large Caps for now. The Russell 2000 has begun to outperform the S&P 500 as leadership turns against mega cap Growth, AI and Tech. The call may be short-term.

Reasons for the Small Cap call: Fed hikes have stopped being added to the forecast, the Russell 2000 is modestly undervalued on P/E, CFTC positioning is deeply net short but shorts are closing, consensus 1H27 earnings growth is stronger than for the S&P 500 AI names, and GDP forecasts and ISM manufacturing have improved.

Small Cap risks: the call needs cyclical excitement (jobs growth, ISM manufacturing, GDP forecasts). Rate hikes, worse conditions in the Middle East, wider high yield spreads or a rising VIX would hurt, and a tier 2 or worse pullback would bring a harder risk-off tone.

RBC's 12-month S&P 500 price target stays at 8,150, which implies 7.5% from the 10/30/26 close. The firm still sees a 5-10% pullback as overdue and possibly underway, which would take the index to 7,000-7,400. The S&P 500 was down about 3% from its all-time high at the 10/30 close.

The fair value model is built on 2.75% CPI, three Fed hikes, 10-year yields of 5% and a 10% haircut to consensus EPS. A stress test with 3% CPI, four hikes and 10-year yields of 5.25% points to fair value slightly above 7,900, which leaves limited upside from the YTD high.

Four tactical risks: the Iran war (re-escalation after the midterms is a risk), downward revisions to 2027 consensus EPS, the midterm elections, and higher rates with a new Fed hiking cycle. S&P 500 drawdowns of about 10% have typically accompanied the start of hiking cycles.

Midterms: Cook Political Report now gives Democrats a slight edge in the Senate in addition to flipping the House. RBC moves the split-Congress signal to 'neutral to positive'. It rates a Democratic sweep neutral to negative and a Republican sweep positive.

Historical midterm stat: the S&P 500 averages +16.9% in the year after a midterm, but only +6.2% (median 3.5%) when neither Q3 nor Q4 of the midterm year was down. RBC argues a longer-term rally may need a dip around the event, and is less enthusiastic than the consensus 'stocks rally after midterms' view.

AI and data centers are a rising campaign issue. Democratic candidates' sentiment has been uniformly negative since August, and Republicans drifted from positive to neutral or slightly negative by late September/early October, around when Tech peaked relative to the S&P 500 (Oct 7). Governor races rank data centers higher than the Senate or House studies do.

RBC warns that the consensus view of low post-election AI regulation risk could be wrong. Battleground states with heavy data center presence (Texas, Ohio) have governor races, and a strong anti-Big Tech outcome could push Congress or state governments to act.

Growth vs Value: RBC sees no basis for fighting the rotation out of big cap Growth. Growth/Value has tracked the 10-year yield recently (yields down, Value outperforms). Nasdaq futures positioning is still elevated but starting to fall.

US vs non-US: the US has lagged non-US developed markets since Oct 7. US P/E relative to non-US is slightly below its five-year average but not yet at the lows that sparked rotations back to the US. RBC does not think the inflection point has been reached.
Earnings: the 3Q26 beat rate for the S&P 500 is 81% on EPS and 65% on sales (35% reported), versus 86% and 76% in 2Q26. S&P 500 upward EPS revisions are slipping toward downward-revision territory.

Consensus S&P 500 trailing EPS is $354 for 4Q26 (from $313 at the start of the year), with 27% y/y growth, slowing to 21% for 4Q27. Net income share of the top 10 names (42.5%) now exceeds their market cap share (41.6%), a gap of -0.9% versus +10.3% in March 2000.

Sentiment and valuation models: the AAII-based sentiment model points to +11.1% over 12 months. The NTM earnings yield gap model points to +14.9% and the FY2 model to +13.4%. The 10-year yield would need to exceed about 6.26% (NTM) for the model to signal negative returns.

Rates: the 10-year yield rose 137 bps from late February to a high of 5.3% on Oct 5 and is now back below 5%. Real yields hit a new YTD high in October. The Fed hiking cycle has just begun, and a 10% pullback has been typical at liftoff, excluding 2022 (range -8.2% to -14.2%, median -9.6%).

Sector views: Overweight Financials and Health Care. Underweight Utilities. Market weight on Communication Services, Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Energy, Industrials, Materials, REITs and Tech. Energy is the best performer since late July. Industrials and Utilities screen most expensive.

Fund flows: Consumer funds had their largest weekly outflow since 2022, as did Utilities and Materials. Health Care sector flows remain positive. Tech flows are positive only because of one earlier spike. Growth funds are seeing small outflows.
Within Tech, Software valuations are attractive and near GFC lows relative to Semis, but Software EPS revisions are starting to slip. Semis FY2 P/E is still well above its long-term average of 18.7.

earnings_insights: 3Q26 S&P 500 reporting season (prelim, as of Oct 28, 35% of companies reported): 81% beating consensus on EPS and 65% on sales, versus 86% and 76% in 2Q26.
3Q26 Russell 2000 reporting season (prelim, as of Oct 28, 16% reported): 64% beating on EPS and 65% on sales, versus 65% and 65% in 2Q26.
Investor reaction to the big TIMT companies that have reported in 3Q26 has generally been weak.

Bottom-up consensus S&P 500 EPS (Bloomberg): trailing four-quarter $354 for 4Q26 (consensus estimate, includes actuals through 3Q), up from $313 at the start of 2026. Consensus y/y EPS growth is 27% for 4Q26 and 21% for 4Q27.
Consensus 2026 EPS growth has ticked down while 2027 has moved up. S&P 500 net income is expected to peak in 2026, and the AI basket is also now expected to see peak growth in 2026.
Consensus 4Q26 net income growth: S&P 500 AI Basket 56%, Russell 2000 49%, S&P 500 28%, S&P 500 ex-AI 19%. For 4Q27: Small Caps 37%, AI Basket 37%, S&P 500 21%, ex-AI 12%.
RBC's price target model uses a 10% haircut to consensus 2Q27 trailing EPS, to about $344 (9% y/y growth versus consensus of 21%), compared with a typical annual trim of about 8%.

charts_described: Table on page 62 shows scenarios for 2Q27 S&P 500 fair value: the current model input (2.75% CPI, 4.50% Fed funds, 5.00% 10-year yield, P/E 23.72) with a 10% EPS haircut gives 8,158, while Stress Test 1 (3.00%, 4.75%, 5.25%, P/E 23.02) gives 7,917.
Page 10 table sets tier thresholds for S&P 500 drawdowns from the 10/6/2026 high: Tier 1 (5-10%) 7,037-7,428, Tier 2 (14-20%) 6,255-6,724, Tier 3 5,317-5,708, Tier 4 about 3,909.
Page 51 chart notes the top-10 S&P 500 names' market cap share was 41.6% versus net income share of 42.5% in late October, a gap of -0.9% versus +10.3% in March 2000.
Page 124 table shows average S&P 500 return the year after midterms of 16.9% (median 18.4%) versus 6.2% (median 3.5%) when neither Q3 nor Q4 was down.
vol_and_positioning: CFTC Russell 2000 positioning is deeply net short, deepest in decades except 2015-2016 and 2022, and shorts are narrowing.
Asset manager positioning in Nasdaq 100 futures is a bit below its peak but not oversold, and appears to be in the early stages of moving lower.
US equity futures asset manager positioning is elevated but not euphoric, and has slipped recently.
AAII net bulls were -3.60% weekly and -3.53% on the four-week average as of 10/29/26, versus -8.90% and -5.60% the prior week. A weekly reading near -24% occurred earlier.
High yield spreads have widened slightly and the VIX has shown signs of life, both negatives for Small Caps relative to Large Caps if they continue.
Momentum fund flows: the largest outflow since 2022 was recorded six weeks ago.
geopolitical: The Iran war: RBC flags that companies may soon feel adverse impacts, and that news reports highlight re-escalation risk after the midterms. The war is tied to oil, 10-year yields, inflation and consumer pressure.
US midterm elections on Tuesday Nov 3, 2026: Democrats favored to flip the House and now slight favorites in the Senate per Cook Political Report.
Possible post-election challenges to results and delayed counts, plus the possibility of a sitting senator switching parties.
Political conditions in France make catalysts for European equities hard to identify.

tension_points.bull_case: The consensus view is that stocks do well after midterms, with the S&P 500 averaging +16.9% in the following calendar year.
tension_points.bear_case: The average falls to 6.2% if neither Q3 nor Q4 of the midterm year was down. Clients doubt there is a policy catalyst, and a Congress focused on investigations is hard to see as a positive driver.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A material dip around the event would make the stronger post-midterm pattern more likely, while no dip leaves returns near the 6.2% average.

tension_points.bull_case: Most investors downplay regulatory risk because of legislative constraints, the idea that anti-AI rhetoric fades after the election, and state and local governments being the main regulators.
tension_points.bear_case: The view is deeply consensus. Governor races in data center states (Texas, Ohio) and bipartisan voter angst could lead Congress or states to act more than assumed.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Exit polling and post-mortem analysis showing AI and data center messaging materially influenced battleground outcomes.

tension_points.bull_case: Hike expectations have stabilized, Small Caps are modestly undervalued, CFTC shorts are closing, and 1H27 consensus earnings growth is stronger than for S&P 500 AI names.
tension_points.bear_case: Valuation is only modestly attractive and never fell to recession lows. Cyclical excitement may be reined in by hikes or Middle East conditions, and wider spreads or a higher VIX hurt Small Caps.
tension_points.what_invalidates: More Fed hikes being added to the forecast, high yield spreads widening, VIX spikes, or a tier 2 or worse pullback.

tension_points.bull_case: Tech valuations have improved to slightly attractive, Software valuations are attractive, and Nasdaq 100 P/Es are back to long-term averages.
tension_points.bear_case: Valuation case is not deep, Semis EPS revisions are decelerating, flows have faded, and the US/non-US and growth leadership trades are breaking down.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A rebound in the rate of upward EPS estimate revisions for Semis and Semi Equipment, and a US/non-US P/E indicator falling well below its five-year average.
